item.title: From Trees to Granite
item.description: The US-China Relations Super Bowl At Halftime
item.dc:creator: Kevin Xu
item.content:encoded:
In May, when Trump visited Xi in Beijing, I compared it to watching the Super Bowl for US-China relations nerds. If that was the first quarter of the championship game, then we just had the second quarter last week, when Xi visited Trump in Washington, with the third and fourth quarters officially booked. (Both leaders invited each other to meet again during the November APEC Summit in Shenzhen and the December G20 Summit in Miami; both cheerfully agreed.)

Much of the coverage and commentary about the second quarter zoomed in on the pomp and pageantry of Xi’s first state visit to the US capital in 11 years, when my old boss Obama was president. By rolling out the literal red carpet, wrinkles and all, every time Xi’s shoes were about to touch American soil, Trump got chided a fair bit by parts of the media he attempted to ban and a good chunk of Congress he wished never existed, for being way too nice to the leader of the world’s biggest communist party. 

The chiding and meme-making started almost immediately, when Trump broke all protocol to personally greet Xi at Andrews Air Force base, launched a few cool American airplanes to show respect (and show off), only to wince at the thunderous flyover while Xi looked unimpressed and jetlagged. Saturday Night Live compared Trump’s eager airport pickup to being “a boyfriend with no job”.

Over-indexing on the goofier side of the coverage would make you think that Trump so desperately wanted Xi to come, while Xi only obliged so Trump would stop texting. A closer look at the timing, circumstance, and how the first quarter in May went down suggests a more mutual affection. 

Lest you forget, the Mid-Autumn festival was also last week, a major Chinese holiday that involves lots of family gathering and mooncake-eating that only the Lunar New Year could rival. Yet, as 1.4 billion Chinese people woke up on the morning of September 25 to celebrate this holiday, their dear leader was halfway around the world in the White House East Room, making toasts and clinking glasses with the American president and tech CEOs. Xi wanted to be there as much as Trump wanted to have him.

This level of commitment from the Chinese side was already on display when Trump visited in May. Remember, Jensen Huang was a last minute addition to the American delegation, the sort of improvisation that’s typical of Trump’s style but rarely tolerated by a more rigid, protocol-heavy Chinese counterpart. Yet, to make things work, China “rolled with it” and Huang attended every official event available to other CEOs and stayed longer in China afterwards to eat street food. Marco Rubio, the secretary of state and featured guest on the Chinese sanctions list, was also allowed to enter China on that visit without any issue, just so he could admire the ceiling of the Great Hall of the People. We still don’t know exactly what legal and diplomatic gymnastics were exercised to render the list temporarily obsolete, but when the leaders want to hang, all lists are pretty obsolete. 

The truth is both sides want these visits to happen as badly as the other and are willing to bend rules and break protocols to make the occasions special, even though neither side wants to let on as much. 

Two Old Men Doing More Stuff

When I wrote a tongue-and-cheek post about the May visit, what struck me was how much time the two heads of the two most powerful countries, one 80-years-young and the other seven years more junior, spent doing normal stuff that old men do. In particular, we saw Xi give Trump a rare tour of the mysterious Zhongnanhai, where Chinese leaders live and work, and most of what they talked about, at least on camera, was how old all the trees were in the yard.

On day one of the US state visit, as Xi’s plane touched down with Trump waiting on the tarmac, I wondered if these two old men would be doing more old men stuff. They did not disappoint. 

On day two, Trump apparently cut his official meeting time with Xi short, because he wanted more time to show Xi stuff around the White House. They toured the West Wing, where Trump showed a large photo on the wall, known in White House parlance as “jumbos”, of him and Xi hanging out in Beijing. 

They walked along the West Colonnade, where past presidents’ portraits are displayed, and made fun of the “auto-pen” portrait at the expense of another old man and democratic traditions writ large. 

Finally, as if to say: “want to see what else I’ve done to the place?”, Trump took Xi out back to check out the newly-constructed helipad that lands the presidential helicopter, Marine One. When mugged by the press after the tour, Trump told the media he tried to ban that Xi “likes granite” and is “an expert on stone, and he loves good granite”, as Xi looked on amused.

Granite is indeed the critical material (though not exactly a rare earth) that was used to build the new helipad, especially the Seal of the President. As for whether Xi ever did have any expertise or strong opinion about granite, Julian Gewirtz found that in 2021, Xi admired the longevity of granite while inspecting a railway project in Tibet. So the personal appreciation for granite isn’t exactly made up. Was this piece of random historical factoid about Xi in Trump’s briefing book though? I have my doubts.

Regardless, the momentum of the US-China Super Bowl has decidedly shifted from touching old trees to feeling old stones that would last a million years, long after either AI or SI wipes out humanity.

On day three, the last day of the visit, the finale was a date at the museum. Here is a video I found of the two old men’s entire 8-minute tour of the National Archive, where both admired the original Declaration of Independence and the Constitution.

The audio and acoustic quality was not as good as the Zhongnanhai tree tour, but it appeared that Xi showed as much interest in learning about the founding documents of the United States of America as Trump showed about the old trees dating back to the Qing Dynasty. At various moments of the tour, Xi leaned in to observe the documents up close. He asked about how many signatures are on the Constitution (he thought he saw 30), to which the museum curator confidently answered, “There should be 54.” 

At one point, unprompted, Trump started admiringly telling his two honored guests, both of whom are in fact Chinese, that China’s history is 6,000 years long (somehow 1,000 years more than the official talking point of the Chinese government), so much longer than the 250 years that America has racked up. After smiling approvingly, and perhaps also to make sure his buddy doesn’t feel too insecure, Xi reciprocated with his own compliment of 250 years of nurturing the American founding spirit (or something, I couldn't hear over the bad acoustic). 

The ritual of two (very powerful) old men doing more stuff together lives on. 

AI G2 Moves Forward

To be fair, some serious business did get done in between the hangouts. 

The ongoing war in Iran was discussed and both sides agreed to agree that Iran should not pursue nuclear weapons, and no country (ahem Iran) can impose a toll on any international waterway (ahem Strait of Hormuz). This agreement ended up being one of the few items that appeared in both of the official statements each country released on accomplishments and deliverables of the trip. Since so many of these statements are intended for a domestic audience, some differences are now expected as these two major countries improve their chemistry with each other. Thus, the more noteworthy items are the shared ones. 

A tariff reduction on non-sensitive goods, worth $30 billion on each side, was also agreed to, though not announced until the Monday after. A picture perfect visit takes precedence over sharing inflation-reducing deliverables. The US list and the Chinese list are both quite wide-ranging in its coverage. Thanks to such a successful trip, America now agrees that Made in China Christmas decorations and plastic plates are no longer sensitive products that pose national security threats. China, on the other hand, can enjoy cheaper and fresher duck innards from a Midwestern farm straight into the spiciest hotpot.

The one development I watched for most closely is whether an AI dialogue between the two technology superpowers will come to fruition. It was hinted at during the May visit when Mythos just launched and scared the living hell out of the world. Since then, we have had more and far scarier events caused by AI agents. With few shared interests, but a growing list of shared risks, I expressed my hope on an NPR interview leading up to Xi’s state visit that the two sides could and should establish some communication channel to manage those shared risks.

It looks like my prayer has been answered, for now.

Both sides agreed to establish an ongoing bilateral dialogue with the next meeting scheduled for November, likely around the APEC Summit in Shenzhen. Both sides also recognized this agreement in their respective statements, another noteworthy shared item. The only difference, to the extent that anyone cares, is that the White House statement called it “the U.S.-China Super Intelligence (SI) Dialogue”, Trump’s preferred way, while the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs statement called it an “AI Dialogue”, everyone else’s preferred way.

As for the actual mechanism of the dialogue and how it would prevent risks in the future, it is scant on details. The only thing we know is that the two principals in charge are Scott Bessent and He Lifeng. I guess if something goes wrong, they will just…call each other? Or text? Or WeChat? Or fax (not a joke, Matt Sheehan made a very good case for faxing on the Ezra Klein podcast.)

If there is a pair of officials between the US and China who’ve spent more quality time with each other than Trump and Xi, it would be Bessent and He, having been the point person on multiple rounds of trade and tariffs negotiations since Liberation Day. Do they have deep technical expertise? No, both are more finance bros than tech bros. Is AI dialogue-ing their full time job? No, not even close. 

But as long as they pick up each other’s calls or texts or faxes when the next swarm of AI agents break out of the sandbox, I guess we can all sleep a little easier.

Who is Winning at Halftime?

With the first two quarters now in the books, who is winning at half time?

The viewers, of course!

For a brief few days last week, we enjoyed some quality political TV that was just wholesome and fun, while temporarily forgetting the historically high treasury rate, the ongoing war in Iran, and more AI agents possibly breaking out of their cells. Even the “30 billion for 30 billion” tariffs reduction deal had the ring of the “30 for 30” ESPN documentary series. If there is any administration that knows good TV, it’s the Trump administration. 

Oh and pandas, two pandas are coming to the Atlanta Zoo! Can’t forget about the pandas. I’m sure Ping Ping and Fu Shuang will be on the field making plays during the second half of this major countries Super Bowl. 

Some experts were disappointed that the pause of retaliatory tariffs that were agreed to in Kuala Lumpur last year and set to expire on November 10th was only extended to January 10th of next year. These experts clearly don’t know how good TV and good sports drama work.

With two more Trump-Xi meetups remaining this year, the finale culminating in mid-December at the G20 on Trump’s home turf of Florida, you need a deadline bearing down on the occasion to heighten the moment and magnify the deliverables. Who cares if businesses can’t find predictability in their cost structure or ordinary families can’t budget their holiday season spending. And like I said before, Xi is just as willing to roll with Trump’s punches, as Trump is willing to give Xi lots of face. The second half will be a sight to see, and we will be glued to our screens for every play. 

Whether you are stuck in the Chinese system of maximum rigidity or opted for the American system of maximum entertainment, most normal people just want their leaders to at least not hate each other so much that their cost of living skyrockets, or their bank accounts get hacked by an AI model, or their children are sent to some foreign land they can’t find on a map to die. If the prevention of these awful things happening hinges on two old men liking each other and regularly doing stuff together, then so be it.

As for me personally, now that I’m a new father with a growing family, I’ve become a forced buyer of all varieties of children’s products. It warmed my heart to see highchairs and all kinds of children’s seats on the “30 for 30” list. I’ll be grabbing a couple of more of those non-sensitive, nationally-secure boosters seats before the game clock turns zero.

item.title: There and Back Again: Tracking Global AI Talent Flow
item.description: Arguably the most often-uttered piece of factoid about the global AI landscape is that China produces 50% of the world’s AI talent. It is a number that Jensen Huang of NVIDIA is fond of repeating in almost every interview he does, and no interviewer has questioned where
item.dc:creator: Kevin Xu
item.content:encoded:
Arguably the most often-uttered piece of factoid about the global AI landscape is that China produces 50% of the world’s AI talent. It is a number that Jensen Huang of NVIDIA is fond of repeating in almost every interview he does, and no interviewer has questioned where that neat, clean number came from. 

In fact, it came from a 2023 study done by the think tank, Macro Polo. As the founder of Macro Polo, Damien Ma, likes to point out, the study actually shows that 46.3% of undergraduate AI talent came from China. That 50% is directionally correct, but also a mild case of “Jensen Math”, which loves to round up.

Nevertheless, the Macro Polo global AI talent tracking which began in 2020 was an insightful, influential, and one of a kind study. I learned a ton from it and wrote about the 2023 update when it came out. So I was disappointed when Macro Polo shut down early last year with the sad assumption that this global AI talent tracker will cease to exist. 

My sadness and disappointment turned into joy and delight, when Damien and his team resumed this study under the Carnegie China umbrella and published an update earlier this week. Just like the last study, it is chokeful of insights and findings that inform arguably the most important yet also the most elusive input into the future of AI: human talent.

Young and Plenty

The big headline takeaway is that China now produces 57.4% of the global AI talent (again, this is based on undergraduate degrees). This is a solid 11% increase from when the study was last done three years ago. (I can literally hear Jensen updating his talking point to “China now produces 60% of the world’s AI talent” in future interviews.)

This increase in young AI talent was viscerally evident when I went to China earlier this year and, along with a group of other western AI researchers and writers, met with almost all the top AI labs in China. One of my top takeaways from the trip was how many “crack interns” we met – young twenty-somethings, all of whom studied in Chinese universities, currently working on their PhD’s, but also working full-time as “interns” in these labs doing real research and experimentation work, not BS intern work. 

The youthful vibe we felt on the trip is confirmed by this more quantitative and rigorous study. The “academia-industry” pipeline in China is real, flourishing, and arguably one of its strongest hidden strengths in AI.

Not only is the volume of talent going up, so is the breadth of institutions where these young talents get trained from. Out of the top 30 institutions that this study tracks, Chinese organizations now account for 12 of them, compared to just 6 from three years ago. Among the top 5 institutions overall, 3 are Chinese universities (Peking, Tsinghua, and Jiao Tong). Among the 12 Chinese institutions on the list, 10 are universities, 2 are companies (ByteDance and Alibaba).   

The US’s share on this top 30 list decreased a bit, but still commands the largest share. American organizations spanning both academia and industry hold 14 out of the 30 spots in 2025 versus 18 in 2022. And if OpenAI or Anthropic allows their researchers to publish something, anything, I’m sure their research would land them on this list. But that is wishful thinking. In the meantime, whether it is on raw young talent production or institutional breathe, it seems that China is gaining on the US.  

 

The rosy prospect sort of ends there for China. America may not be producing most of the talent, but it is the biggest magnet and destination for those talents by a long shot. China, on the other hand, is losing the most talent to other countries after putting in the work and resources to educate them. 

On this chart, the US and China are occupying the literal opposite end of the spectrum. The US had a net gain of +2,145 AI researchers in 2025, while China suffered a net loss of −1,729 AI talent. (This is within the sample universe that the study was conducted, which is the NeurIPS 2025 conference published paper authors.) To add insult to injury, half of the Chinese talent who leave China wound up in America. Singapore’s 2nd place spot on this list likely also came at the expense of China, since the trend of “Singapore washing” has been under way for a few years now. 

The Chinese brain continues to be drained overseas.

This massive talent flow towards the US should be somewhat intuitive and unsurprising, if you work in the AI industry or monitor it closely. The American AI industry is by far the most competitive, well-capitalized, and loosely-regulated. This dynamic environment naturally attracts the best and most ambitious AI talent from around the world, whether it is for the money or for the challenge (or both). And since China produces more than half of the young raw talent, a lot of them would be drawn to the US for those reasons, despite a generally more hostile environment towards all immigrants and an increasingly specific suspicion towards Chinese technical talent working or studying in the US.  

When will America’s hostility towards outsiders and foreigners (loosely and ethnocentrically defined) end up shooting itself in the foot in its pursuit of AGI is hard to tell. So far, at least backward looking to what happened in 2025, Team USA is muddling along fine.  

Join Interconnected Premium

Willing Stay or Forced Retention

Brain drain (or brain gain) aside, one surprising finding from the study is how less fluid the talent flow has become with more people staying to work in their home country (or at least home company, since the chart is based on employer's headquarters location).  

This “higher retention rate” is observable in South Korea, Europe, and also China. I think this trend will also continue as sovereign AI takes a stronger hold on how AI will evolve globally. I was originally a sovereign AI skeptic, thinking it was nothing more than a clever sales pitch to sell more chips. While the sales-y side remains true, I have come around to the reality that exerting sovereignty and control over AI is a legitimate strategic and national imperative that all countries will, sooner or later, pursue. I noted this change in my opinion two years ago, shared my updated thoughts with The Economist two months ago, and the drumbeat of sovereign AI has been louder than ever across both countries and companies.

But what has been missing in the sovereign AI discussion is the critical importance of native talent as a key input. The focus so far has been on physical and digital control of AI infrastructure: build local data centers, provide tight security around the data centers, produce own chips or at least buy them from friendly countries, use open weight models, secure data like national treasure to be used and controlled for future AI model development. These are all important elements on the road to real AI sovereignty. But what good does indigenizing the most advanced open weight model and constructing the most secure data center do, if you don’t have the people, ideally people you can call your own, to operate, support, and improve your national AI over time?

I suspect this motivation to control your own talent in service of AI sovereignty is leading to this national retention rate going up. I suspect it will continue to go up in the future. However, how this “sovereignty over talent” gets implemented is worth thinking about. Some of this retention is likely done through a combination of improving domestic opportunities, increasing resources and incentives, plus a healthy dose of appealing to national pride – the carrot. The more punitive way is exit ban, travel control, and even prosecuting your own citizens, however talented they might be, for working for foreign companies – the stick.

We already see headlines of China implementing exit bans of citizens who may know or hold important know-how’s on AI or executives from leading AI labs needing government approval to travel abroad. The Manus acquisition by Meta was thwarted by the government and the startup’s founders were not allowed to leave China until the deal was officially dead. 

South Korea is even more draconian in this regard, having expanded its espionage provisions in its criminal law to prevent leakage of semiconductor technologies. The South Korean government has brought almost 100 cases over the last several years related to technology leakage, many of which involve its own citizens. I have a feeling that these tough measures and chill effects moved the needle more than a little bit in boosting the retention rate observed in the chart above. 

Are more top AI talent staying home willingly or being forced to? How does the scarcity of AI talent influence a country’s overall AI, education, and industrial policy? Is the free flow of talent and knowledge a feature of human advancement we should embrace or a bug of national security that we should reduce? 

These are all extraordinarily important and difficult questions that this study highlights, but cannot answer. As we look to future updates of this study, and hopefully more studies like it, even the source of data is being challenged by national borders and geopolitical tension over talent. As mentioned before, this Carnegie China study leverages paper publication authorship data from the 2025 NeurIPS conference, which had to host the event in both San Diego and Mexico City, where the latter location is a backup plan for researchers, predominantly those from China, who could not secure a US visa. This year’s conference almost excluded publication submissions from all organizations that are on the US entity list, which China’s Association for Science and Technology protested against, and the decision was rolled back, for now.

If the draw bridge is threatened to be pulled up on even academic conferences, the most fluid and innocent form of human talent exchange, the hope for more talent flow among companies, industries, and governments is dim.     

Tech, especially the Silicon Valley version, is fond of rebranding The Lord of the Rings references, but mostly the dark ones – Palantir, Andúril, the Eye of Sauron. There is another Tolkien throughline that is more wholesome, adventurous, and taps into the inner goodness and natural curiosity of humanity. The prelude to the war and destruction of The Lord of the Rings was, after all, Bilbo Baggins’s memoir, There and Back Again. It was a chronicle of the hobbit’s ventures outside his comfort zone, explorations of foreign lands (and a dragon) in the rest of Middle Earth, who returned to the Shire on his own free will to share his stories and treasures with the folks at home.

It is hard to imagine and pointless to romanticize top AI talent doing their own version of There and Back Again these days, freely flowing and roaming to whichever company or country to fulfill his or her curiosity and ambition, but also leaves room for homesickness and ancestral familiarity, if craved. But I’m glad that at least the definitive study that tracks this story is back again.
